title: The Last House
premise: Paloma Dunmore hosts a late-night radio show in the dying village of Hollowmere, where her callers are all people who died the week before—and she documents every call, believing that recording the dead is a form of prayer. When the church bell, melted down in 1911, rings across the moor, Paloma learns the village's founders bound something beneath Hollowmere with a ritual of names, and the binding is failing because no one remembers the dead anymore. To save what remains, she must complete the founders' unfinished rite by speaking every forgotten name aloud at the ruined bell tower—but the price is her own memory of the man she loved, who died last week and has been calling her nightly. In the end, Paloma finishes the ritual, Hollowmere's dead rest, and she survives with a notebook full of entries she can no longer read, keeping the show on air for listeners who never call again.
about_author: Sable Almeida is the pen name of a former night-shift radio producer from coastal Yorkshire who spent years reading obituaries on air before turning to fiction. Their work explores grief as architecture—how we build rooms inside ourselves to house the dead.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She opens her 3 a.m. show to an empty studio in Hollowmere, where the transmitter barely reaches the valley. A caller named Edith describes her own funeral from last Tuesday. Paloma doesn't hang up; she writes it all down. Emotional beat: eerie calm masking loneliness—the documentation habit established as devotion.

chapters.title: The Caller Log
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Over three nights, more dead callers phone in: a drowned boy, a farmer, a woman who asks Paloma to tell her daughter the garden needs watering. Paloma cross-references parish records and confirms every death. Beat: compulsion deepens into purpose; she begins to believe the calls mean something.

chapters.title: Static Where the Bell Was
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Walking home past St. Brannoc's ruins, she hears a bell toll though it was melted down in 1911; only a stump of tower remains. The sound leaves her ears bleeding slightly. Beat: first intrusion of the supernatural into her controlled, documented world—fear arrives.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with interleaved 1890s ledger excerpts. In the archive she finds the Hollowmere Founding Society's ledger: a 'Rite of Names' binding something called the Undermoor, requiring all villagers' names spoken annually at the bell. The last entry is 1910—incomplete. Beat: dread of inherited obligation.

chapters.title: A Voice She Knows
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Her caller that night is Tomas, the man she loved, dead six days in a car crash on the moor road. He speaks gently, asking her not to finish whatever she's started researching. Beat: love against duty crystallizes; her hands shake over the notebook.

chapters.title: What the Village Forgot
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: elderly caretaker Ambrose Vell, the last person raised on the old rites. He confronts Paloma, having heard the bell too. He explains the binding weakens each year fewer people remember the dead. Beat: reluctant alliance; the stakes widen beyond Paloma.

chapters.title: Names in the Walls
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Exploring the bell tower's foundations, she finds founder names scratched into stone, half eroded—except one gap where a name was deliberately chiseled out. That night, callers begin forgetting their own names mid-sentence. Beat: escalation; the erosion is spreading to the living.

chapters.title: The Chiseled Name
chapters.summary: Ambrose's POV. He confesses his family were the founders' servants and keepers: the erased name belongs to Maren Dunmore, Paloma's ancestor, who refused the rite in 1911 and demanded the bell be melted rather than let the thing below feed on remembrance. Beat: Paloma's inheritance is a betrayal—or a mercy.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The radio begins broadcasting without her: her own voice reading names she's never written. Listeners—living ones, a handful left—call in terrified. Tomas begs her to stop documenting, warning that every entry feeds the thing below. Beat: her prayer may be its food; crisis of faith in her method.

chapters.title: The Drowned Boy's Map
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The drowned boy caller guides her through static to the flooded quarry where the bell metal was dumped. Diving, she finds the bell intact beneath the water, un-melted, covered in names. Beat: revelation—the melting was a lie; the bell waits, wanting to be rung.

chapters.title: Ambrose's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ambrose's POV. He offers himself to the Undermoor as a substitute anchor, as his family did for generations, buying the village another decade. Paloma refuses to let him. They fight. Beat: the price of survival made explicit; duty versus compassion between allies.

chapters.title: Silence on the Frequency
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The dead stop calling. The show runs to pure static. Hollowmere feels hollowed—people wander, unable to recall their children's faces. Tomas's voice is gone too. Beat: desolation; Paloma realizes the silence means the binding has nearly failed.

chapters.title: Maren's Letter
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Hidden in her grandmother's sewing box, a letter from Maren Dunmore: she erased her own name because the rite required a Dunmore to ring the bell and be taken below as its voice. Maren fled instead, dooming the village to slow decay. Beat: Paloma understands her destiny is a debt, not a curse.

chapters.title: The Rite Assembled
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Paloma and Ambrose reconstruct the full ceremony from the ledger, the wall scratches, and the letter: gather every name, living and dead, carry them to the quarry, raise the bell, ring it once per name. Ambrose insists on going with her. Beat: grim preparation; resolve hardening into acceptance.

chapters.title: The Living Roll Call
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She broadcasts one final show, asking the living of Hollowmere to speak their names and the names of their dead on air. Dozens call. The notebook fills. Tomas's voice returns briefly to say goodbye. Beat: communal tenderness; the village remembering together as an act of love.

chapters.title: Down to the Water
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At dawn she and Ambrose haul the bell from the quarry using the founders' winch, still rusted but holding. The water resists—hands in the current, whispers offering her Tomas back if she turns away. Beat: temptation at maximum; love against duty at its sharpest.

chapters.title: The First Ring
chapters.summary: Ambrose's POV. Ambrose rings the first stroke and the Undermoor answers: the ground breathes, shadows pour uphill toward them. He holds the rope while Paloma reads names. Beat: terror and awe; sacrifice beginning in real time.

chapters.title: Every Name But One
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She reads through the night—hundreds of names, the bell tolling each, the darkness receding stroke by stroke. Then the ledger shows the rite requires the ringer's own name last, spoken by another. Ambrose steps forward. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of survival.

chapters.title: Tomas's Last Call
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The radio crackles alive one final time: Tomas, calling from wherever he is, asks to read the last name himself. He says 'Ambrose Vell,' then says 'Paloma Dunmore'—not as sacrifice, but so the bell will know her as its keeper, not its victim. Beat: love expressed as release, not possession.

chapters.title: The Voice Below
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Undermoor rises one last time, wearing the faces of everyone forgotten, and offers her the choice: ring the final stroke and forget everything she documented, or walk away and let Hollowmere die remembered-only-by-her. She rings it. Beat: climax; the price paid willingly.

chapters.title: Morning, Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Sunlight. The bell stands whole in the restored tower. Villagers wake remembering their dead with warmth instead of grief-fog. Ambrose lives, aged but anchored. Paloma opens her notebook and cannot read a word of her own handwriting. Beat: bittersweet resolution; survival's cost made intimate.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue. Months later, she still hosts the 3 a.m. show. No one calls—but she keeps the line open, keeps talking to the dark, because even without memory, the habit of listening remains, and that too is a kind of prayer. Final line: 'This is Hollowmere. I'm here.' Beat: quiet hope; love outlasting memory itself.
